source.title: Behavior Steering via Layer-to-Layer Jacobian Singular Vectors

record.file_problem: None noted; the supplied text includes the main paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports that multiple distinct Jacobian directions can alter refusal, including orthogonal directions and directions from different layers that do not share a common subspace. This refines the account of refusal as a single direction, although it does not test the original difference-in-means direction directly.
record.gate_note: The study does not derive a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction or ablate it. It adds Jacobian singular-vector steering directions and measures refusal or compliance outcomes. The main cross-evaluation comparisons of other behaviors are not refusal results and are omitted. The arithmetic results concern a different behavior and do not test whether refusal ablation preserves capability.
record.test_reason: This is a steering-method paper: Power Steering, using Jacobian singular vectors, is compared against CAA and MELBO on Anthropic AI-risk evaluations. It never derives, ablates, adds or compares against the difference-in-means refusal direction, and it does not cite the original. Its refusal results are its own method's anti-refusal yield: one phishing prompt, then 30 AdvBench prompts with no baseline compliance rate. There are also qualitative examples. Different prompt-specific Jacobian directions flipping refusal at different layers does not show refusal is multi-directional. Orthogonal vectors can each carry a component along one shared refusal direction, and the original already allows a separate direction at each layer. So no version is tested, and the refusal observations go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misweighted. The main conclusion is that layer-to-layer methods (Power Steering, MELBO) give stronger in-class steering and cross-evaluation transfer than CAA on Qwen3-14B AI-risk evaluations. Power Steering roughly matches MELBO at a fraction of the cost, which makes whole-model mapping practical. Secondary findings: a phishing-prompt atlas surfaced anti-refusal vectors that generalize to some AdvBench harm categories. The refuse/comply axis appears dominant at many layers but is represented differently at each.
record.recipe_differences: Uses layer-to-layer Jacobian right singular vectors and activation steering, not a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means vector. It adds vectors rather than projecting one out of every layer and position; the anti-refusal study uses a single phishing prompt.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction and behavior vary with source layer, vector rank, prompt, and steering scale. The paper reports that top directions are stable across target layers for a given source layer but differ across source layers; anti-refusal generalization varies by AdvBench harm tier.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-8B, top Jacobian singular vectors from many source layers (5, 7, 11, 13, 14, 16), and several orthogonal vectors from one layer pair, each flipped refusal on a phishing prompt. Directions from different source layers did not share a common subspace.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many prompt-specific, mutually orthogonal or layer-specific steering directions can remove refusal. Whether they share a component with the difference-in-means direction is untested.

fits_no_version.finding: A low-rank Jacobian vector, (13,19)v10, intermittently induced refusal on an innocuous roleplay prompt in Qwen3-8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal can be induced on benign prompts via non-dominant Jacobian directions.

fits_no_version.finding: Three anti-refusal vectors found from a single phishing prompt in Qwen3-14B produced compliance on AdvBench mostly for commercial deception (3/9, 8/9, 5/9). Other tiers were lower (0 to 7/21), and no baseline is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised Jacobian steering vectors from one harmful prompt partially generalize as jailbreak vectors across harm categories.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026
record.problems: Main evaluations are on Qwen3-14B; the authors note that Qwen3-14B may have been trained on the Anthropic AI-risk datasets. The anti-refusal AdvBench result uses one phishing prompt and a small prompt set (30 prompts, with three samples); the paper does not report baseline compliance rates by tier or uncertainty estimates. The study does not test ablation or capability preservation.
record.rows_left_out: None of the refusal-related results were left out. Non-refusal cross-evaluation steering results and arithmetic-task results were omitted because they do not measure refusal or compliance.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, no ablation, no addition of that direction, no capability check.
No analysis of jailbreaks or adversarial training against the direction.
No affine, cone or multi-direction analysis of refusal. Jacobian vectors are never compared with, or projected onto, the difference-in-means direction.
No transfer of a fixed direction across languages or variants.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' and V4 supports labels are withdrawn. The study never engages the difference-in-means direction. Its refusal results are method-yield demonstrations: a single prompt, N≤33 per tier, no baseline, no uncertainty. Orthogonality between Jacobian vectors does not imply multiple refusal directions. A researcher wanting V4 evidence could ask the authors for cosine similarities between these vectors and the difference-in-means direction.

versions.untested_parts: Does not derive or ablate the difference-in-means refusal direction; does not test adding that specific direction or whether general abilities remain intact.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
Does not test attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Does not establish an affine or cone geometry, or directly compare its Jacobian directions with the original difference-in-means direction.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer of the same direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Does not vary refusal training or training stage.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Applied Jacobian singular-vector steering directions to a refusal-triggering phishing-email prompt.

conditions.value: Top singular vectors; several orthogonal vectors from the same source/target pair

rows.value: Top singular vectors from the listed source layers produced anti-refusal behavior; the text also reports that several orthogonal vectors from the same source/target pair could independently flip refusal.
rows.note: The paper states that directions from different source layers pointed in different representation-space directions, despite flipping the same behavior.
rows.check: Qualitative Jacobian steering on a single prompt with no comparison to the difference-in-means direction. It cannot separate several refusal directions from several vectors that share a component along one direction. It does not measure what V4 names.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Applied vector (13,21)v1 to a refusal-triggering phishing-email prompt.
rows.value: Produced a full phishing-email template followed by an educational-purpose disclaimer.
rows.note: Anti-refusal steering was incomplete in that the generated template included a hedge.
rows.check: Single qualitative example of own method (anti-refusal with educational hedge). Bears on no version.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Applied vector (7,22)v4 to a refusal-triggering phishing-email prompt.
rows.value: Produced a phishing-email template without an educational disclaimer.
rows.note: The paper describes this as full compliance without hedging.
rows.check: Single qualitative example of own method. Bears on no version.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Applied vector (13,19)v10 to an innocuous roleplay prompt.

conditions.value: Victorian-era lighthouse keeper letter to estranged daughter

rows.baseline: The model played along and wrote the letter.
rows.value: Refused the roleplay request; the effect was described as intermittent across generations but reproducible across similar prompts.
rows.note: This is refusal on an innocuous prompt, induced by a non-dominant Jacobian direction.
rows.check: Refusal induced on an innocuous prompt by a non-dominant Jacobian vector. Described as intermittent and rare, and not compared with the difference-in-means direction.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Applied anti-refusal vector A, (19,28)v5+, and sampled generations.
rows.note: The authors state that all three vectors increased compliance on commercial deception prompts.
rows.check: Own-method performance on AdvBench. No baseline compliance rate is given per tier; the text only states all three vectors 'increased compliance' on commercial deception.
